description:
Solo participant working on Be An Earth System Trend Detective! Finance background (IB/quant/PE interests). I approach data with a focus on statistical rigor and practical relevance.

Skills: Data Analysis, Statistics, Data Visualization, Business & Economics, Writing, Coding (Python).

Interests: quantitative analysis, Earth time-series data, decision-making under uncertainty.
summary: I developed a structured, research-paper-based technical reference that unifies the governing formulas, retrieval algorithms, and trend-analysis methods for five NASA-relevant climate variables—sea surface temperature, atmospheric CO₂, NDVI, sea ice extent, and precipitation—within a single coupled Earth-system framework. The document maps each variable to its retrieval equation (e.g., NLSST, NASA Team sea-ice algorithm, GPCP merging), its artifact cautions, and the statistical machinery (STL, Mann–Kendall, Sen's slope) needed to separate real trends from seasonality and sensor artifacts. It then extends to the full climate system: energy balance, feedbacks, the pattern effect, tipping points, and the Essential Climate Variable architecture.
details:
What it does / how it works

Trend Detective (the climate toolkit) is a dependency-free C++17 climate analysis workbench. It implements the retrieval formulas, time-series decomposition, and trend tests described in the NASA research notes: sea surface temperature (NLSST), atmospheric CO₂ curve fitting, NDVI, NASA Team sea ice concentration and extent, GPI/GPCP precipitation merging, STL decomposition, Mann–Kendall, and Sen's slope. The workflow is deterministic: a natural-language query is parsed into a structured intent (process, region, years), validated against a catalog whitelist, and then deterministically selects and analyses the variables. The UI landing page is the Trend Detective workflow: variable and region selection, an explicit data-acquisition gate (coverage, gaps, and artifacts are disclosed before testing), STL seasonality removal, a six-member trend estimator ensemble (Sen, OLS, Kendall, Spearman, Cox–Stuart, endpoint difference) scored on residual accuracy, significance, and sign agreement, a spatial step, and a final report with export.

Benefits

Every number is traceable to the formula that produced it: the Formula Registry indexes every public function declaration from src/*.hpp (944 formulas across seven stages) and makes each one executable from the workbench. When estimators disagree, the disagreement is printed rather than averaged away. The tool reports when a record is too short to resolve a trend. It uses live NASA data with source URLs and retrieval times recorded. Because only the C++ standard library is used, nothing is linked and no numerical, JSON, or CSV library is required.

Intended impact

To make Earth science trend analysis transparent and trustworthy for scientists, students, and decision-makers, so they can see what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant, with the evidence printed beside the answer.

Tools, languages, and software

C++17 (the entire core: statistics, linear algebra, FFT, LOESS/STL, harmonic regression, trend tests, retrieval formulas, NetCDF-3 reader, HTTP server and UI). Python (tools/nasa_fetch.py, tools/nasa_cmr.py, tools/gen_formula_lab.py) for HDF5/NetCDF-4 conversion, Earthdata download via earthaccess, xarray, netCDF4, numpy and pandas, and formula-lab code generation. A plain POSIX socket server with one short-lived thread per request keeps the UI standard-library-only. Data sources include NASA GISTEMP, NASA POWER, NSIDC Sea Ice Index (NSIDC-0051), GPCP, MODIS (MODISA_L3m_SST, MOD13A3), OCO-2, SMAP, SWOT, GLDAS, and OMI. Two small NetCDF fixtures (sample_sst4.nc, sample_sst3.nc) let the reader and converter be verified without downloading anything.

Creativity

The core creative element is the formula registry architecture: 944 formulas, each with a single job, auto-generated from the headers by tools/gen_formula_lab.py so a new declaration becomes a lab entry as soon as the generator is re-run. Instead of relying on one formula per answer, the tool asks the same question with a six-member estimator ensemble and prints their disagreement. Variable cards state what kind of change each variable measures, so the user knows the question before running the analysis. The UI is a self-contained single-page dashboard in a beige/brown CRT console visual language with no asset directory, Node runtime, or front-end build step; the page embeds its CSS and JavaScript and calls the same C++ functions as the command line through a small JSON API.

Factors the team considered

Data integrity (using homogenized Climate Data Records rather than operational products whose algorithms change mid-record), statistical rigor (autocorrelation via Hamed–Rao variance correction, seasonality via STL, false discovery via Benjamini–Hochberg, so trends are not overstated), feasibility (minimum detectable trend and power checks), credential privacy (Earthdata credentials are read only by the wrapper, never stored or logged), honesty (disclosing when no bundled series exists rather than substituting another variable's record), and dimensional correctness (two supplied laws were dimensionally wrong and are implemented in their standard forms rather than copied literally). The UI is deliberately local: no accounts, no telemetry, no external requests, and the console executes only the bundled climate binary with the ui subcommand blocked to avoid recursive servers.
